title: Supervision, behaviour rules and drowning prevention at home pools
audience: Pool service technicians who visit home pools and must give owners drowning-prevention advice in writing
learningOutcomes: Describe the supervision rules for children and non-swimmers at a home pool and state which ones a service worker can enforce
Identify the handbook rules on diving, horseplay, depth marking and glass near the pool
Explain why no cover, gate or device is treated as a complete drowning control
Record drowning-prevention advice given to an owner and the points that need the owner's action

instruction.heading: Drowning is the main hazard at a home pool
instruction.body: A home pool is a drowning hazard before it is a cleaning job. Water can be dangerous even in shallow depth, and a small child can drown in a small amount of water. The UK handbook behind this lesson makes the point that the most effective defence is constant supervision, teaching and common sense, not one device. Your visit is a chance to look at the safety arrangements and to tell the owner what they must keep doing. You do not take over supervision during a visit, and you do not assume that a barrier is adequate because it exists. Note what you see, tell the owner, and refer barrier questions to the owner or to the relevant authority.

instruction.heading: Supervision and the people who use the pool
instruction.body: Every member of a household should be taught to swim as early as is practical. Small children should be kept away from the water unless an adult is present, and they should enter only when an adult says they may. Adults watch swimmers continuously while the pool is open for use, and that includes older swimmers. Watching people in the water is not the same as keeping the whole pool in view, so the rule is that a named, responsible adult watches the water continuously. Never allow small children to swim unsupervised. Visitors' children should come onto the grounds only by invitation and when an adult has agreed to supervise them.

instruction.heading: Behaviour rules at the pool
instruction.body: The handbook sets rules you can check and reinforce on a visit. Ban horseplay and bombing, do not run around the edge of the pool, plus do not push or hold other people under the water. Dive only from the designated place, which is the place designed for diving. Mark the deep and shallow ends clearly, and display diving prohibitions where the pool has no designed diving area. Keep glass containers and glass products beyond the pool edge surround, because broken glass causes cuts and can enter the water. These rules only protect people when they are enforced, so record which rules the owner's household is not following on the day.

instruction.heading: What a barrier cannot do on its own
instruction.body: Gates, covers, alarms, moving floors and fences all depend on people. A gate has to be closed and locked, a safety cover has to be placed over the pool once nobody is using it, and a moving floor has to be locked in position. The handbook states that no single product is a foolproof safety device. Treat every barrier as one layer and never describe a pool as safe because it has a cover, fence or device. Barrier design, height, gate and alarm requirements are set by state, territory and council rules. The pool-standards lessons that cover them are not part of this set.

instruction.heading: Clear water is a safety condition
instruction.body: The water needs to be clear enough to see the whole bottom at all times. If you cannot see the bottom, the pool must not be used until the cause is found and corrected. Poor clarity can come from low filtration, unbalanced chemistry or a filter that needs cleaning, and the handbook links clarity directly to safety. Report the cause to the owner or operator. Do not decide that a pool is usable because the surface looks acceptable from the edge.

instruction.heading: Insurance and written advice
instruction.body: The handbook suggests that the owner ask an insurer about public liability cover for the pool plus its equipment. Give the owner drowning-prevention advice in writing, date it, and record the owner's response. Do not give legal or liability advice.

procedure: Look at the barrier, gate and cover and record their condition. Do not certify them.
Check for depth markings, diving signs and any glass items near the poolside.
Confirm the bottom is visible at the deepest point before any work starts.
Ask who is responsible for supervision during the visit and record that person's name.
Give the owner the drowning-prevention points from this lesson in writing.
Refer barrier, registration and insurance questions to the owner, the operator or the relevant authority.
Record what you saw, what you advised and what the owner agreed to do.

workedExamples.situation: The family asks you to leave the gate open so the pool cleaner can move in and out. Two young children are playing near the fence while you work.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not leave the gate open, and do not assume the children are being watched. Ask a responsible adult to take charge of the children and close the gate behind you. Record the request, the adult's name and the action taken. Tell the owner that a gate works as a barrier only when it is closed and locked.

workedExamples.situation: The owner says the pool is 'safe' because it has a safety cover and asks you to write that on the invoice.
workedExamples.reasoning: A cover works as a layer only when it is in place. Do not write whether the pool is complete safe or certified. Write what you saw on the day, whether the cover was in place, and the advice that a cover does not replace supervision. Supervision applies regardless of whether the cover is on.

equipmentAndPpe: Visit checklist for barriers, gates, covers and signage
Torch for checking depth markings and the lower edges of the pool
Written drowning-prevention advice sheet from the operator or owner (this is not a certificate)
Camera or phone to record the condition, where the owner agrees
Gloves for handling glass or debris near the edge

commonErrors.error: Certifying the pool as safe or compliant
commonErrors.prevention: Record observations only. Compliance decisions belong to the authority and the operator.

commonErrors.error: Treating a cover or gate as the whole control
commonErrors.prevention: Describe each device as one layer that depends on people using it.

commonErrors.error: Working while children are unsupervised near the water
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, ask a responsible adult to take charge, and record the time.

commonErrors.error: Accepting clarity seen from the edge as proof the bottom is visible
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the bottom can be seen at the deepest point before work starts.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Stop work and raise the alarm if anyone is in difficulty in the water. Follow the site emergency procedure and call emergency services where needed.
Avoid using the pool at the time the floor is not visible at every moment.
Do not allow visitors' children onto the grounds without an invitation and an adult in attendance. Never allow small children to swim unsupervised.
Keep glass products beyond the pool edgeside. Broken glass near the pool causes cuts and can enter the water.
Water can be lethal in small depth. Treat every pool and spa as a drowning risk regardless of size.
This lesson grants no authority to inspect or certify a barrier.
Check insurance requirements, including public liability, with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

qualityStandard: A named adult is recorded as responsible for supervision during the visit.
Each drowning-prevention point given to the owner is recorded with its date and the owner's response.
No barrier, cover or device is described as complete protection or as compliant.
documentationEvidence: Visit note with barrier observations, recorded as observations rather than certifications
Dated written advice given to the owner
Referral record for barrier, registration or insurance questions
Incident or near-miss report where a child or swimmer was at risk
summary: Drowning prevention depends on continuous supervision and on people following simple rules.
Covers, gates and devices are layers that depend on people to use them.
If the floor cannot be made out, stop work and refer.

knowledgeChecks.question: A homeowner says the pool has a safety cover, so no one needs to supervise during your visit. What is the correct response?
options: Agree, because a cover is a complete safety control and the owner has paid for it
Explain that a cover is only one layer and that supervision still applies whenever the pool is open
Ask the owner to remove the cover so you can judge whether the pool is safer today
Write on the record whether the pool is complete certified safe and sign it for the owner

knowledgeChecks.question: Which handbook rule is a service worker most likely to need to reinforce on a visit?
options: Keeping glass containers near the poolside so they are easy to reach
Letting children swim alone while the owner is in the house
Banning horseplay and bombing, and keeping the depth markings clear
Diving from any part of the pool to test the depth

knowledgeChecks.question: When can work start at a pool where the water surface looks clean from the edge?
options: Once the water has been cleared of surface debris from the edge and the owner has checked the depth
Once the filter gauge reads normally and the pump has been running for an hour
Once the owner confirms the water is fine and the crew has seen it from the edge
Once the bottom can be made out clearly at every moment, including at the deepest point
